insight: ingredients.js PAC/POD derivation ANDs a validity check across 7 sugars including galactose; USDA routinely reports only 5 (no galactose), so the gate almost always fails and PAC/POD are silently left unpopulated. Treat absent galactose/maltose as 0, not as invalid.

The sugar to PAC/POD formula exists twice: ingredients.js:781 takes fractions (0-1), tools.js:174 takes percents (0-100). Same math, 100x apart. Change one and the PAC/POD calculator silently disagrees with the USDA importer.

office-hours Phase 5 writes {user}-{branch}-design-*.md with the raw branch name, so a branch containing / creates a subdirectory. plan-eng-review sanitizes / to - and globs flat, so it reports No design doc found. Write the design doc with the branch slashes already replaced by dashes.

npm test runs node test-app.js, a 1624-line custom Playwright harness with 24 methods and 116 logTest assertions, all via page.evaluate against a live server. testNoConsoleErrors filters type===error only, so console.log spam passes. No pure-function unit lane exists.

CORRECTS usda-pacpod-galactose-gate. The PAC/POD gate fails because of nutrient NAME mismatches, not galactose coverage. FDC returns Glucose (not Glucose (dextrose)) and Total Sugars (not Sugars, Total NLEA). getNutritionValue returns -1 on no match and fails silently, so Sugar never populated either. Measured 0/11 pass with current names, 6/11 with corrected names.

To decide whether an incomplete FDC sugar breakdown is safe to derive from, sum the individual sugars present and compare to Total Sugars. If it reconciles within tolerance the absent sugars are genuinely zero (honey reconciles to 0.03g while reporting no lactose). Beats any hardcoded safely-zero sugar list: self-validating, no chemistry table to maintain.

FDC Foundation records carry Water/Fat/Energy but no individual sugars and no Total Sugars. SR Legacy carries the full sugar profile. ingredients.js:714-735 prefers Foundation, so for formulation it selects the record that cannot produce PAC/POD.

gstack _gstack_codex_auth_probe reports AUTH_OK and CODEX_MODE: ready whenever OPENAI_API_KEY or CODEX_API_KEY is merely non-empty. Codex CLI 0.147 does NOT read those env vars: it needs the key stored via `printenv OPENAI_API_KEY | codex login --with-api-key`, which writes ~/.codex/auth.json. With the var set but no login, codex returns 401 Missing bearer or basic authentication in header while the probe still says ready. Smoke test with a trivial `codex exec` before trusting the probe.

~/.codex/auth.json is container-local in Claude Code on the web, so codex authentication does not survive container recreation even when OPENAI_API_KEY is set in the environment config. The SessionStart hook must re-run codex login on every cold start.

/review SKILL.md reads .claude/skills/review/checklist.md, but in a symlinked install ~/.claude/skills/review/ contains only a SKILL.md symlink. The real files (checklist.md, greptile-triage.md, design-checklist.md, specialists/) live at ~/.claude/skills/gstack/review/. Read from there instead of stopping on the missing path.

IceEd.html is a frozen 3528-line snapshot of the original monolithic app (documented as a backup in STRUCTURE.md, STACK.md and MODULARIZATION_PLAN.md). It carries its own copy of the ingredient data, the Sugars table and the USDA import, so any fix in js/ leaves it stale. Do not patch it: it is a historical record. Check STACK.md deployment claims instead.

Async hooks are configured with an "async": true FIELD on the hook handler in .claude/settings.json, plus "timeout". Printing {"async": true, "asyncTimeout": N} from the hook script does NOTHING -- the script stays synchronous and the JSON is just stray stdout. Also set a "matcher" (e.g. "startup"): with no matcher a SessionStart hook fires on startup, resume, clear, compact AND fork, so expensive setup re-runs mid-session. gstack office-hours/session-start templates teach the stdout-JSON pattern, which is wrong. Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

Do not use Math.max to pick between alias nutrient names in the USDA import. getNutritionValue scans foods in Foundation > SR Legacy > Survey order and returns the first match, so each single name already respects record priority. Math.max across aliases picks the numerically larger value regardless of which record it came from, so one ingredient profile can be assembled from two different USDA records. Use ordered first-match (firstNutritionValue) instead.

When falling back across alias names AND across priority-ordered records, the loop nesting decides correctness. Records must be the OUTER loop and aliases the INNER loop. Alias-outer looks equivalent but exhausts every record for the first alias before trying the second, so a lower-priority record matching the primary name beats a higher-priority record matching the alias. Caught by cross-model review after a first fix got the nesting backwards.

Validating a numeric shell input with ^[0-9]+$ is not enough: a value like 999999999999999999999999999999 matches but overflows bash signed 64-bit arithmetic, so every [ -ge ] errors with integer expression expected and a bounded wait loop becomes infinite. Bound the digit count and range-check.

Do not validate a shell variable with grep -qE. grep matches LINE BY LINE, so a multiline value like $(printf "1\ninvalid") passes on its first line. Use a case statement, which matches the whole string: case "$v" in ""|*[!0-9]*) reject;; esac. Also bound magnitude BEFORE arithmetic (long digit strings overflow bash 64-bit ints and make every -ge error), and strip leading zeros so 00000 is understood as 0. This defect recurred three times in one session, each time in a different form.

Iterated cross-model adversarial review on this branch converged 5 -> 3 -> 3 -> 0 findings across four passes. Passes 2 and 3 were essential: two pass-2 findings were defects the pass-1 fixes introduced, and pass 3 caught the third variant of a bug fixed twice. Re-running after each fix round is worth it until a pass comes back clean; a single pass would have left five P1s partly unfixed and two new ones added.

Stating a decision in three sections of a design doc (Scope, Correction narrative, Implementation Tasks) guarantees drift: when measurement changed the design, two of three got updated and six passages were left describing abandoned approaches, including one instructing a future implementer to use the exact pattern a later review had removed. Make ONE section authoritative for buildable detail (the task list), keep rationale separate, and freeze dated correction narratives as never-edit.

A single percent-populated success criterion becomes unevaluable the moment a feature can produce estimated values: the same implementation scored 91% counting estimates and 73% excluding them. Split into measured-rate and derived-rate, and treat the gap (estimate rate) as a watched signal rather than a target, so the metric cannot be passed by guessing more.

This repo has no VERSION file and versions via package.json semver (3-digit). gstack-version-bump classify therefore returns DRIFT_UNEXPECTED, whose documented handling is STOP-and-reconcile. That is a false positive: there is nothing to reconcile, the repo simply never adopted the 4-digit scheme. Bump package.json directly and continue. Decided 2026-08-11 to keep one version source.

/ship Step 20 writes ~/.gstack/projects/$SLUG/$BRANCH-reviews.jsonl using the raw branch name. Branch names containing a slash (claude/foo, feature/bar) make that a nested path and the append fails with No such file or directory, silently losing the ship metrics. Sanitize with tr / - first, matching what gstack-slug and the plan-file lookup already do.

The batch loop (recipe -> churn -> outcome -> improved recipe) cannot be built without recipe versioning underneath it. A batch observation attached to an unversioned recipe is unattributable, because the formula can change silently after the fact. The Jan 2026 versioned-recipes todo already contains the hard thinking (lock vs float, npm package.json/package-lock analogy) and is the floor, not a competing item.

Finding that no competitor ships a feature is not automatically white space. Six mature ice cream formulation tools, several paid, none built a batch log. That is either a gap they all missed or a verdict from their users. Treat competitive absence as a question to test, not evidence of opportunity, especially when your own demand evidence is N=1.

Before designing a digital replacement for a manual workflow, get the actual mechanics of that workflow in detail. The Ice Ed founder was assumed to have unlinked batch notes; in fact he runs a working version-control system out of a printer and a 3-ring binder (versioned names, print as immutable snapshot, annotate during churn, copy-and-tweak for the next version). That correction inverted the design from replace-the-paper to feed-the-paper, and removed the largest risk (behaviour change at capture time). Ask how the workaround works mechanically, step by step, not just what it costs.

When an app prints a form that gets annotated by hand and photographed back, do NOT frame the return path as OCR. Split by technique: (1) identity via a printed QR/DataMatrix encoding record+version, decoded with BarcodeDetector or jsQR -- essentially perfect, no backend; (2) structured outcomes via optical MARK recognition on checkboxes and scales at positions the app itself chose -- Scantron-era reliability, plain canvas pixel sampling, no backend; (3) handwritten prose -- Tesseract.js explicitly excludes handwriting, cloud HTR needs an API key and therefore a backend, so store the photo and display it instead. Tiers 1 and 2 deliver most of the value with none of the risk.

Converting a prose capture habit into checkboxes and scales makes data queryable but can reduce what gets recorded. A conditional observation (icy only at the edges, better after two days) does not fit a 1-5 scale, and that qualified detail is often the one that leads somewhere. Before designing a structured form to replace free text, measure the existing prose-to-marks ratio in the real records rather than assuming structure is an upgrade.

Before designing any feature that attaches metadata to an existing entity, verify the save/load round-trip actually preserves unknown fields. In Ice Ed both directions filter: save rebuilds the container from a fixed shape (recipe-manager.js:1195) and load copies only keys already declared on a fresh model instance (app.js:284). A design can specify a parent pointer, a diff and a photo reference in detail and every one of them silently vanishes on the next load. Read the serializer before the schema.

An existing @media print block does NOT mean an app can produce an immutable printed record. Ice Ed print is btnPrintRecipe.onclick = () => window.print() (recipe-manager.js:1400): it renders the live DOM including unsaved edits, so a printed page can show a formula that was never persisted. Any design where the printed artifact is the record of truth needs print to persist an identified snapshot first. Separately, optical mark recognition needs @page, physical units and registration marks; a variable-length table moves every mark coordinate.

When a review adds a prerequisite phase, check the new phase for internal dependency cycles before publishing it. The batch loop Phase 0 listed "copy primitive that mints a new identity" and "print an identified snapshot" BEFORE the task that creates identity, and before the batch entity being identified. Prerequisites reorder the graph, so re-derive the whole order rather than prepending tasks to the front of the old list.

A guard conditioned on current state ("refuse rename only if this recipe has descendants") is unsound whenever another actor can change that state later. Offline device holds the old name; the renamed recipe gains a child; the device reconnects and republishes. The guard could not have known. In a name-keyed sync there is no window where the conditional check is sound, so make the restriction unconditional or fix the identity model. Applies generally: guards over distributed state must be unconditional or backed by reconciliation.

In a static web app with no forced upgrade, a stale cached tab is a legacy CLIENT that can write. Ice Ed hydrates only known cRecipe fields (app.js:284) and rebuilds the saved container from that truncated object (recipe-manager.js:1195), so an old build silently strips any new field from a record a new build created -- and sync runs automatically on sign-in (sync-manager.js:36). Storing new metadata in a SEPARATE object store fixes this without operational rules: a client cannot erase a store it does not know exists.

Never edit a document with python str.replace without asserting the replacement happened. It returns the unchanged string on a non-match and reports nothing, so an amendment can be committed, announced as landed, and simply not be there. This happened twice in one session on the same paragraph, and was caught only by an outside reviewer reading the file. Use the Edit tool (fails loudly on non-match) or assert old in s before replacing, and grep for the NEW text afterwards rather than checking unrelated invariants.

Moving metadata into a separate object store to protect it from legacy clients solves the downgrade-write problem and creates a distribution one: in Ice Ed sync transfers only recipe.data (sync-manager.js:122) and Drive stores {name, data} with no sidecar (google-drive-storage.js:53), so a second device finds no identity and allocates its own. A protective sidecar has to travel with the thing it describes. Also: keying such a store by a mutable name reintroduces delete-and-reuse collisions; key by id with a name index.

codex exec (0.147) can hang indefinitely at the websocket handshake to the OpenAI API through the container proxy: no session rollout file is created, no error is printed, and it never recovers. Healthy runs finish in 20-60s even for large review prompts. Never wait long: run with timeout ~150s and retry up to 4x, logging stdout/stderr to files. A missing rollout file under ~/.codex/sessions/ = stalled transport, not slow reasoning. Not client-side, not auth, not rate limits: verified 2026-08-12 when 4 of 7 invocations hung while interleaved small and identical-retry runs succeeded. OpenAI had a declared API/Codex error incident the prior evening; sub-threshold recurrence indistinguishable from proxy websocket issues from inside the container.

A version/schema guard that type-checks before comparing fails OPEN: containerSchemaVersion mapped any non-number SchemaVersion to 1 (legacy), so a string "2" bypassed the newer-schema refusal and silently truncated -- the exact loss the guard existed to prevent. Three independent review passes converged on it. Rule: absent = legacy; present numeric or numeric-string = its value; present garbage = refuse (corruption is not legacy). The codebase precedent that made string versions realistic: the .ier envelope check uses loose != and its tests pin that "1" is accepted.

The roundtrip harness injected a private IngredientsMap via getIngredients while importIngredients mutates ingredients.js module-level Ingredients -- in the app these are the SAME object. So library-intact assertions inspected a map the load path never touched, and the merge-conflict path could never fire. When a harness mirrors app wiring, inject the REAL module singletons (seeded per test), not lookalike private copies. Found by red-team review, not by the 35 passing tests.

Refines codex-websocket-flaky-retry-short. The failure correlates with RUN DURATION, not prompt size and not the -s flag: every sub-30-second codex run today succeeded (6s smoke tests always; a 20s inline-analysis prompt), while every run needing 60s+ of streaming (file-reading reviews) hung with zero output and no rollout file. One 2-minute file-reading review did succeed at 14:40, so it is probabilistic per connection-second rather than a hard block, and the rate degraded through the afternoon. Practical consequence: codex is usable for short questions and NOT usable for repo-reading reviews in this container. Do not burn turns retrying a review prompt; a successful smoke test does NOT predict a review will complete.

Immutable-snapshot fixes must capture the record IDENTITY at the same instant as the payload, not just the payload. P0.5 froze the container at click time but kept reading Recipe.Name live across two awaits, so a rename during an IndexedDB read stored the record under one name while its snapshot claimed another, made the exists-check ask about a different key than the write targeted (unconditional put = silent clobber of another recipe), and let the local and cloud writes sample the name independently. Reproduced end to end. Rule: after taking a snapshot, derive EVERY downstream value from the snapshot, including keys and user-facing messages.

Object.freeze THROWS on typed arrays with elements (Cannot freeze array buffer views with elements) even though structuredClone accepts them and IndexedDB stores them natively, so adding a deep freeze to a save path can turn a perfectly storable record into a total refusal of both Save and Export. deepFreeze also only walks Object.keys, so Map/Set/Date survive cloning and stay mutable inside a supposedly frozen snapshot. Verify a freeze against every type the clone step preserves, and never let the immutability step be the reason data cannot be written.

Any field added inside recipe data syncs for free (sync moves only data, sync-manager.js:122) but is INVISIBLE to the sync join, which runs over listRecipes() {name,updatedAt} summaries only -- Drive names come from filenames (google-drive-storage.js:141-151). Also: Drive updateFile uses uploadType=media which never rewrites appProperties, so a metadata mirror of any body field can silently go stale. Both bit the P0.3 identity design.
